I haven't seen the TPP, and would like to see it as much as you would, but there is one big way I know of that influence in Asia could help working class Americans.

China has been accused of artificially inflating its currency. What this mean is it makes it cheaper (much cheaper) for companies to hire people in China than hire people in America. China likes this because they have hundreds of millions of high-school educated workers to keep employed. This was also good for America for a while (as in, when the working class American used to go home with disposable income at the end of the week) because it let us buy things we needed, like microwaves and computer parts, at a lower price. The problem is it prevents Americans from being employed at higher rates, because the low-skill jobs are in China. It also makes China's money less valuable, so workers in China have less money to spend on American goods, and Americans have less jobs making things that can be sold on the world market.

As I said. I have no idea if this is in TPP. We should be able to look at it and have it explained to us. But there are reasons why it's good to have better trade relations with major world markets.

I actually think the article did a good job or explaining it. Some of a companies value it determined by assets. They purchase assets in places with low tax rates to push their value up and therefore avoid the taxes on those assets even though they provide market value to the company. They can also set up online portions of their company to push transaction through these locations, and claim that they occurred there, taking advantage of those tax laws. Many transactions occur this way, including some in-store ones, because of where the actual processing of the transaction occurred. They can also do this with other types of holdings, such as patents, trademarks, subsidiaries and shipping portions of their company, choosing nations that are more favorable to their position--things bought online can be deferred to areas of the company that operate in the UK, Canada, etc. and then shipped over the border to customers in other nations, saving them money. I'm sure there are many other, more sophisticated ways of doing it, but these are some of the ones I have identified. Is it technically illegal? Yes it is? do major companies get away with it because they have truck loads of cash? Yes.
